evidence.source: 字源 (李學勤主編; 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692)
evidence.field: PDF p. 87; printed p. 75; headword entry and scan-verified passage
evidence.text: The scan shows the headword 口 and its reading note. The entry calls it a pictograph shaped like a human mouth, says its basic meaning is ‘mouth’, cites an oracle-bone occurrence and the poem 詩·豳風·鴟鴞 using 口 in its basic sense, and notes that bronze inscriptions also use it as a clan sign. It describes ancient forms as generally two strokes and says three-stroke writing may appear by Han times, with stroke order differing from modern practice. I inspected the original scan pixels for the headword, forms, cited lines, and the entry’s ending before 囑. The account supports the mouth pictograph; the stroke-history statement is the book’s proposal, not independently confirmed here.
evidence.title: 字源 (PDF scan; edition details verified against the book’s copyright page)

evidence.source: 漢字「口」：字形演變, Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The record groups 口 examples under oracle-bone, bronze (including 集成05413), Chu manuscripts, small seal, and Shuowen, and explains the graph as depicting a human mouth with upper and lower lips, used for eating and speaking. This independently supports the basic pictographic account, while the page’s form group labels alone do not establish a precise stroke-by-stroke development sequence.
evidence.title: 漢字「口」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry describes 口 as an open mouth and cites an oracle-bone use in 合集13642, 疾口, as referring to illness of the mouth. It also records bronze uses as a clan name and as 曰 ‘say’. The source separately distinguishes the downward-facing component 亼 (‘inverted mouth’) from frontal 口 and cautions that they have different component functions. This offers a useful boundary: meanings assigned to a mouth-like element in compounds should not automatically be transferred to 口.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 口

evidence.field: 康熙字典 / 國語辭典書證
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen’s “人所以言食也。象形” and lists a Han-period citation from 王充《論衡·道虛》 using 口 for a container opening, plus 《孟子·梁惠王上》’s 數口之家 for household population. These attest those uses in the cited works, but do not establish when either extension began or a semantic path from ‘mouth’.
evidence.title: 口 kǒu - 漢典

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry gives the Shuowen definition and the same Han-period vessel-opening citation, and lists senses for a bodily mouth, passage, barrier, blade edge, break, and person-counting classifier. It confirms the dictionary tradition’s glosses and citations; it does not date their origins or establish their derivation.
evidence.title: [A00480] 口 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The inspected local row gives kMandarin kǒu. This is current reading metadata, not evidence for the graph’s formation. The official character-specific Unicode Unihan page was attempted but inaccessible in this research session, so no official click-through record is available here.

gaps: The 字源 scan’s cited oracle-bone text and the 甲/合集 examples are referenced in print, but this pass did not inspect the original inscription artifact images; exact earliest attestation remains unresolved.

The claim in 字源 that two-stroke forms predominate in ancient writing and three-stroke forms may appear by Han times is visible in the scan but was not independently verified across source inscriptions.
The dictionary citations document opening and household-population uses but do not establish their earliest occurrences or semantic development from ‘mouth’.
